layers.authority: Ministry of Home Affairs, Government of India; foreigners' permits issued through the Leh District Tourist Management System (LAHDC Leh and District Administration Leh)
layers.process: The area between the Inner Line and the international border is a Protected Area under the Third Schedule of India's Immigration and Foreigners Order 2025. The Inner Line runs about a mile north of the Zoji La, Dras, Kargil, Khalsi, Nimu and Leh road, so places such as Pangong, Nubra, Khardung La and Tso Moriri need a Protected Area Permit. Leh's administration takes foreigners' applications online at lahdclehpermit.in and encourages applying through a local travel agent. Citizens of Pakistan, Afghanistan, China, Myanmar and Sri Lanka, Taiwan and Hong Kong passport holders, and foreign nationals of Pakistani origin need their permit from the Ministry of Home Affairs in New Delhi. Smartraveller advises applying at least 4 weeks ahead.

layers.authority: LAHDC Leh and District Administration Leh
layers.process: Tourists visiting Leh pay a fee made up of an environmental (green) fee, a Red Cross Fund contribution and a wildlife fee. Pay online on the Leh District Tourist Management System; applying through a local travel agent gives 10% off the total fees. The portal warns of fake environment fee slips.

layers.authority: Ministry of Home Affairs, Government of India (e-FRRO portal)
layers.process: The Sonamling Tibetan settlement near Leh (Choglamsar, Agling, Spituk and camps in Changthang such as Nyoma, Sumdo and Hanle) is a Restricted Area under the Fourth Schedule. Daytime visits are allowed without a permit if the settlement, monastery or institute gives the visitor's name, parentage, date of birth, nationality, passport and visa numbers to the Foreigners Registration Officer. Staying needs a Restricted Area Permit; foreign students can get one valid for 3 years if the institute vouches for them.
